# Including phylogenetic uncertainty - Julia version

Often, we do not have a single phylogeny but a set of phylogenies, e.g., from a Bayesian phylogenetic inference. When using phylogenetic control, we want to marginalize over the phylogenetic uncertainty. Doing this in R + Stan is possible but cumbersome and computationally expensive. Therefore I will explore re-implementations of the R/Stan models in Julia + Turing.jl, and in Python + NumPyro.

Let's start with Julia.

```{julia}
# Create data directory if it doesn't exist
isdir("../data") || mkpath("../data")

# Paths
tgz_url = "https://github.com/rbouckaert/global-language-tree-pipeline/releases/download/v1.0.0/all_trees.tgz"
tgz_file = "../data/all_trees.tgz"
tar_file = "../data/all_trees.tar"
tree_dir = "../data/all_trees/"

# Download and extract
if !isdir(tree_dir)
    Downloads.download(tgz_url, tgz_file)

    # Decompress .tgz to .tar
    open(tgz_file) do f_in
        open(tar_file, "w") do f_out
            write(f_out, transcode(GzipDecompressor, read(f_in)))
        end
    end

    # Extract .tar archive
    Tar.extract(tar_file, tree_dir)
    # Move all files from ../data/all_trees/all_trees to ../data/all_trees
    inner_dir = joinpath(tree_dir, "all_trees")
    if isdir(inner_dir)
        for f in readdir(inner_dir; join=true)
            mv(f, joinpath(tree_dir, basename(f)); force=true)
        end
        rm(inner_dir; force=true, recursive=true)
    end
    # Clean up
    rm(tgz_file)
    rm(tar_file)
end


# Load all Newick trees
tree_files = glob("*.tree", tree_dir)

trees = [parsenewick(read(f, String)) for f in tree_files]

# Optionally strip suffixes
for tree in trees
    for tip in getleaves(tree)
        tip.name = split(tip.name, "_")[1]
    end
end
```

## Vanilla regression

We will use the same model as in the previous notebook, but now we will use Turing.jl to implement it.

The likelihood is implemented as a Turing model like this:

```{julia}
#| vscode: {languageId: julia}
@model function vanilla_regression(x, y)
    N = length(x)
    # Center x
    means_x = mean(x)
    Xc = x .- means_x

    # Priors
    alpha ~ LocationScale(0, 2.5, TDist(3))
    beta ~ Normal(0, 2)

    # Linear predictor
    η = alpha .+ beta .* Xc
    
    # Likelihood
    for i in 1:N
        y[i] ~ BernoulliLogit(η[i])
    end
    
    loglik := [logpdf(BernoulliLogit(η[i]), y[i]) for i in 1:N]
    y_rep := [rand(BernoulliLogit(η[i])) for i in 1:N]
end
```




Let's run the model:

```{julia}
#| vscode: {languageId: julia}

# Run the model with actual data
@time begin
    chain_vanilla_regression = sample(
        vanilla_regression(d.x, d.y),
        NUTS(),
        MCMCThreads(),
        1000,
        4,
        discard_initial=1000,
        progress=true,
    )

end
# Print summary of the chain
describe(chain_vanilla_regression[:, [:alpha, :beta], :])
```

The 95% credible intervals for the parameters are:

```{julia}
#| vscode: {languageId: julia}

hpd(chain_vanilla_regression[:, [:alpha, :beta], :])
```


```{julia}
#| vscode: {languageId: julia}
# plot the posterior distributions of alpha and beta

ridgelineplot(chain_vanilla_regression, [:beta], title="Posterior distributions of beta")

```

This looks reassuringly similar to the R/Stan model. Now let's plot the prior and posterior predictive distributions.

```{julia}

function predictive_checks_regression(y_rep, y_prior; d=d)
    obs_0 = mean(d.y[d.x.==0])
    obs_1 = mean(d.y[d.x.==1])
    # Define colors
    CBblue = RGB(0.0, 114 / 255, 178 / 255)
    CBvermillion = RGB(213 / 255, 94 / 255, 0.0)

    p0 = density(y_prior[d.x.==0],
        fill=(0, 0.5, CBblue),
        label="Prior",
        title="P(y=1|x=0)"
    )
    density!(p0, y_rep[d.x.==0],
        fill=(0, 0.5, CBvermillion),
        label="Posterior")
    vline!(p0, [obs_0], color=:black, label="", linewidth=2)


    p1 = density(y_prior[d.x.==1],
        fill=(0, 0.5, CBblue),
        label=false,
        title="P(y=1|x=1)"
    )
    density!(p1, y_rep[d.x.==1],
        fill=(0, 0.5, CBvermillion),
        label=false
    )
    vline!(p1, [obs_1], color=:black, label="", linewidth=2)


    link = :both
    plot(p0, p1, layout=(2, 1), link=:x, legend=:topleft)
end

```

Next we sample from the prior and the posterior. In Turing, this is fairly straightforward.

```{julia}
# Prior predictive sampling - sample from prior with missing y
model_prior = vanilla_regression(d.x, fill(missing, length(d.x)))
prior_chain = sample(model_prior, Prior(), 4000)

# Posterior predictive sampling - use the fitted chain

y_rep_names = [v for v in names(prior_chain) if occursin("y_rep", string(v))]

y_prior = mean(Array(prior_chain[:, y_rep_names, :]), dims=1) |> vec

y_rep = mean(Array(chain_vanilla_regression[:, y_rep_names, :]), dims=1) |> vec
```

```{julia}
predictive_checks_regression(y_rep, y_prior)
```

Next we compute the marginal log-likelihood and the LOOIC.

```{julia}
#| vscode: {languageId: julia}


function create_logdensity_function(model)
    # Create a LogDensityProblems-compatible object
    logdensity_obj = DynamicPPL.LogDensityFunction(model)

    return function (params::Vector{Float64})
        # Use LogDensityProblems.logdensity instead of DynamicPPL.logdensity
        return LogDensityProblems.logdensity(logdensity_obj, params)
    end
end

```

```{julia}
#| vscode: {languageId: julia}
# Compute log-likelihood
logdensity_func_vanilla_regression = create_logdensity_function(vanilla_regression(d.x, d.y))


```

```{julia}

samples_vanilla_regression = [Vector(chain_vanilla_regression[:alpha][:]) Vector(chain_vanilla_regression[:beta][:])]

```

```{julia}
#| vscode: {languageId: julia}

function bridge_sampling(
    samples::Array{Float64,2},
    log_density::Function
)
    nr = size(samples, 1) ÷ 2
    samples_4_fit = permutedims(Array(samples[1:nr, :]))
    samples_4_iter = permutedims(Array(samples[(nr+1):end, :]))
    r0 = 0.5
    tol1 = 1e-10
    n_post = size(samples_4_iter, 2)
    m = vec(mapslices(mean, samples_4_fit, dims=2))::Vector{Float64}
    V = diagm(ones(size(samples, 2)))
    q11 = Vector{Float64}(undef, n_post) # unnormalized posterior
    @threads for i = 1:n_post
        q11[i] = log_density(Array(samples_4_iter[:, i]))
    end
    q12 = Vector{Float64}(undef, n_post) # g
    @threads for i = 1:n_post
        q12[i] = logpdf(MvNormal(m, V), samples_4_iter[:, i])
    end
    gen_samples = rand(MvNormal(m, V), n_post)
    q21 = Vector{Float64}(undef, n_post) # unnormalized posterior
    @threads for i = 1:n_post
        q21[i] = log_density(gen_samples[:, i])
    end
    q22 = Vector{Float64}(undef, n_post) # g
    @threads for i = 1:n_post
        q22[i] = logpdf(MvNormal(m, V), gen_samples[:, i])
    end
    l1 = q11 - q12 # samples_4_iter, unnormalized posterior / g
    l2 = q21 - q22# gen_samples, unnormalized posterior / g
    lstar = median(l1)
    n_1 = length(l1)
    n_2 = length(l2)
    neff = (1.0 * n_1)::Float64
    try
        neff = minimum(summarystats(sim).value[:, end, 1])
    catch e
    end
    s1 = neff ./ (neff .+ n_2)
    s2 = n_2 ./ (neff .+ n_2)
    logr = log(r0)
    log_r_vals = [logr]::Vector{Float64}
    logml = logr + lstar

    function upd(logr)
        lognumi = logsumexp([
            l2[i] - lstar - logaddexp(log(s1) + l2[i] - lstar, log(s2) + logr) for
            i = 1:size(l2, 1)
        ])
        logdeni = logsumexp([
            -logaddexp(log(s1) + l1[i] - lstar, log(s2) .+ logr) for
            i = 1:size(l1, 1)
        ])
        log(n_1) - log(n_2) + lognumi - logdeni
    end

    ft = optimize(y -> (upd(y) - y)^2, -10000., 0.)
    ft.minimizer + lstar

end
```

```{julia}
#| vscode: {languageId: julia}
# Compute marginal log-likelihood
logml_vanilla_regression = bridge_sampling(samples_vanilla_regression, logdensity_func_vanilla_regression)
println("Marginal log-likelihood: ", logml_vanilla_regression)
```

```{julia}
#| vscode: {languageId: julia}

# Alternative: Create a more structured view of LOO results
function format_loo_results(loo_dict)
    # Extract the main metrics
    estimates = DataFrame(
        metric=["LOOIC", "SE of LOOIC", "elpd_loo", "SE of elpd_loo"],
        value=[
            loo_dict["looic"],
            loo_dict["se_looic"],
            loo_dict["elpd_loo"],
            loo_dict["se_p_loo"]
        ]
    )
    return estimates
end

```

```{julia}
#| vscode: {languageId: julia}


@model function vanilla_correlation(x, y)
    N = length(y)

    # Priors
    mu ~ MvNormal(2, 2.0)
    L_R ~ LKJCholesky(2, 1.0)

    # Latent variables: raw standard normal vectors
    # Sample standard normal
    z_std = Matrix{Float64}(undef, 2, N)
    for n in 1:N
        z_std[:, n] ~ MvNormal(I(2))
    end

    # Transform outside the sampling statement
    z = L_R.L * z_std .+ mu

    # Likelihood
    for n in 1:N
        x[n] ~ BernoulliLogit(z[1, n])
        y[n] ~ BernoulliLogit(z[2, n])
    end

    # Compute correlation from the correlation matrix
    R = L_R.L * L_R.L'
    rho  := R[1, 2]
    mu1 := mu[1]
    mu2 := mu[2]
end


```

```{julia}
#| vscode: {languageId: julia}

@time begin
    chain_vanilla_correlation = sample(
        vanilla_correlation(d.x, d.y),
        NUTS(),
        MCMCThreads(),
        200,
        4,
        discard_initial=200,
        progress=true,
    )

end
# Print summary of the chain
describe(
    chain_vanilla_correlation[:, [:mu1, :mu2, :rho], :]
)

```

# Prior and posterior predictive sampling for vanilla_correlation

Computing the marginal log-likelihood and LOOIC for the correlation model:

```{julia}
# Compute log-likelihood
logdensity_func = create_logdensity_function(vanilla_correlation(d.x, d.y))

N = length(d.x)
samples = Array(chain_vanilla_correlation)

logml = bridge_sampling(Array(chain_vanilla_correlation), logdensity_func)


println("Marginal log-likelihood: ", logml_vanilla_correlation)


```
